passage: I was on the terrace at Kabir's birthday when I noticed Pema holding the same cup of lime soda for an hour. Two of the boys kept holding out a bottle. "Just one, don't be boring," one said, and the other laughed. Pema smiled, shook their head and said, "No, I'm good, thanks." The bottle came back twice more. Pema's smile got smaller and their eyes kept going to the stairs. I can't say what Pema was thinking. Around eleven, Pema said, "Early class tomorrow," picked up a bag and left without any fuss. Next day I saw Pema in the canteen with the quiz club, laughing loudly over tea. Nobody at that table asked about drinking. I took the empty chair and joined in. Varun

qa.q: What did Pema hold for an hour at the party?
qa.a: Pema held the same cup of lime soda for an hour.

qa.q: What might Pema have been feeling as the bottle came back twice more?
qa.a: Possibly torn and uneasy, since Pema's smile got smaller and Pema's eyes kept going to the stairs, though Varun says the inner state can't be known for sure.

qa.q: What could Pema do if friends keep pushing next time?
qa.a: Say a simple no, leave early as Pema did, and spend more time with people like the quiz club who don't pressure.

qa.q: How might the boys who offered the bottle have seen the moment?
qa.a: They may have thought they were joking and including Pema, without noticing that "don't be boring" felt like pressure.

grounding: Friends push a drink with 'don't be boring'; Pema says a simple no, leaves early and finds easy company.

passage:
Nilesh, sit down, I see that face. They called you boring at the party, didn't they? Let me tell you about your Avni aunty at nineteen, in the hostel in Pune. My roommates had a bottle every Saturday. First they offered. Then they teased. "Avni, you're so boring. Just one sip, just to be one of us." I felt torn in two. I wanted to belong so badly. I also knew I didn't want it.

One night I said, very simply, "No, I don't drink. I'm going to sleep." No speech. One of them rolled her eyes. I went to bed early, heart thumping.

The next month I joined the college trekking club. On the first climb, a girl called Farida shared her water and said, "Good, someone who'll actually remember the view." We're still friends. Thirty years.

qa.q: Where did Avni aunty stay at nineteen?
qa.a: She stayed in the hostel in Pune.

qa.q: How did young Avni feel when her roommates teased her?
qa.a: Young Avni felt torn, badly wanting to belong but knowing she did not want to drink.

qa.q: What choice inside the story made the biggest difference?
qa.a: Saying a simple no without a speech and then joining the trekking club, where Avni found people who liked her sober.

qa.q: How might Farida have seen Avni on that first climb?
qa.a: Farida seemed glad to meet someone who didn't drink, and saw Avni as good company rather than boring.

grounding: The elder's story shows a young woman pushed to drink to fit in who says a simple no, leaves early and finds friends who accept her sober.

passage:
The fest ended at eleven, but the last bus back to the village left at ten, and Harish had already missed it twice this semester. Behind the auditorium his friends were passing around a bottle.

"Harish, one drink. Don't be a grandmother." Everyone laughed. Someone pressed a paper cup into his hand.

He felt his face heat. These were the boys he'd eaten lunch with for a year. He didn't want to lose them, and he didn't want the drink.

"No, I'm fine. I've got the bus." He handed the cup back.

"Boring!"

"Yeah," he said, and smiled, and walked away.

At the bus stand he found Rekha from his statistics class, also waiting. "Escaped too?" she asked. They talked about the dance performance all the way home. Next week she invited him to the college photography club.

qa.q: What time did the last bus to the village leave?
qa.a: The last bus left at ten.

qa.q: What was Harish feeling when the cup was pressed into his hand?
qa.a: Harish felt torn and embarrassed, not wanting to lose his friends but not wanting the drink either.

qa.q: How did Harish handle the pressure, and why did it work?
qa.a: Harish said a short, simple no, gave the cup back and left early, without arguing, which let him keep his choice without a fight.

qa.q: How might Rekha see Harish at the bus stand?
qa.a: Rekha seems to see someone like herself who also left, and she welcomes him by inviting him to the photography club.

grounding: The story shows a young man pressured to drink to fit in who says a simple no, leaves early and meets someone who likes him sober.
